questions.q: Which body-plan is stronger for 'Exam Stress': (a) three paragraphs each saying stress is harmful, or (b) causes → effects → coping strategies?
questions.a: (b) — distinct angles advance the article; restating the thesis thrice adds words, not development. A wrong answer shows the student equates length with development.

questions.q: Which opener is article-grade: 'Every night, a million students stare at glowing screens until 2 am — and call it studying' or 'This article is about exam stress'?
questions.a: The first — a scene-setting hook with a claim embedded. The second announces the article instead of beginning it.

questions.q: Is 'Exams are literally destroying our generation, no cap' acceptable in a school-magazine article?
questions.a: No — articles permit voice but hold semi-formal register; 'literally/no cap' slang breaks it. A wrong answer shows over-correction from formal to casual.

questions.q: The class 12 article adds ______ depth: title + byline → hook intro → body paragraphs each advancing a distinct angle (causes, effects, solutions) with examples → a takeaway conclusion.

Fill in the blank: The class 12 article adds ______ depth: title + byline → hook intro → body paragraphs each advancing a distinct angle (causes, effects, solutions) with examples → a takeaway conclusion.

Fill in the blank: The angle-map keeps ______ distinct: a 'digital distraction' article runs causes (notification design), effects (attention metrics), solutions (digital hygiene) — each paragraph owns one angle with an example.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student writes an article with a hook opening, distinct-angle body paragraphs supported by examples, and a forward-looking conclusion — controlling voice within semi-formal bounds.
